opus-5.5.text:
That's a question I've thought about a lot, honestly. When I was finishing my PhD, the obvious path was to join one of the big companies. Many of them were already using vLLM heavily, and the offers were attractive: good resources, a stable environment, and you can still contribute to open source on the side.

But I kept coming back to one thing. vLLM had grown much faster than anyone expected. It went from a research project to something a large part of the industry relies on for inference. Once a project reaches that scale, the question isn't only "how do I personally contribute?" It becomes "who takes long-term responsibility for this thing?" Open source infrastructure needs people who can work on it full-time, think about the roadmap, and do the unglamorous work. That means maintenance, hardware support, releases, community management. If everyone who cares about it is working inside a different company, each with its own priorities, the project can drift or fragment.

So for me, starting a company wasn't really about chasing a business opportunity first. It was more that this project needs a stable home and a team that's fully aligned with keeping it open and healthy. A company can be that vehicle. It can hire engineers to work on it, take on the hard problems that no single user wants to fund, and stay neutral across different hardware vendors and model providers.

Of course there's risk. A job gives you certainty, and a startup gives you none. You also have to figure out how to build a sustainable business around open source without betraying the community, and that's a tension many people have struggled with. I don't think I've fully solved it. But I asked myself which choice I'd regret more in ten years. Missing the chance to shape the inference layer during this particular moment in AI felt like a much bigger regret than giving up a comfortable job. Moments like this don't come around very often, so in the end the decision felt fairly natural.

r001.rationale: The response mentions startup risk and giving up a comfortable job, but does not state that the worst-case cost of failure was a few years of forgone salary.

r002.rationale: The response says vLLM needs long-term responsibility, full-time support, and a stable home, and that starting a company can provide that support.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I didn't treat it as a binary choice at first. When I finished my PhD at Tsinghua, I had the usual options in front of me — go to a big company, join a research lab, maybe a university position. And then there was this thing I had been pouring most of my waking hours into, which was vLLM.

The way I thought about it was, where does my marginal contribution matter most? If I join a large company, I'm one more very capable engineer in a very capable organization. The project moves forward with or without me. With vLLM, it felt different. By that point I had been maintaining large parts of the codebase, dealing with the distributed inference side, the torch.compile integration, a lot of the hardware backend plumbing. The community was growing faster than the number of people who could actually keep the project healthy. So the leverage was obvious. A few people deciding to make this their full-time thing could change the trajectory of something that thousands of companies depend on.

The second question was simply, how do you get paid to do open source? That's the uncomfortable part. People love open source, but love doesn't pay salaries or GPU bills. I looked at a few models. One is you take a job at a company that is a heavy user and they let you spend part of your time on upstream. That works, but your priorities ultimately get set by that company's roadmap, and vLLM has to serve everyone — NVIDIA, AMD, Intel, the Chinese chip vendors, cloud providers, startups. Neutrality is actually a feature of the project. The other model is you build an entity whose whole reason to exist is the project. That's harder and riskier, but it keeps the incentives aligned.

I also want to be honest that there's an emotional component. When you've spent two years with a codebase, you know where all the bodies are buried. Walking away felt like abandoning something unfinished. And there's a window — the inference layer is being decided right now. In a few years it will be settled, one way or another, and the question of who gets to shape that will be closed.

So I weighed stability against leverage and timing, and leverage and timing won. I told myself the downside is bounded. If it doesn't work, I have a very good résumé and I've learned things you can't learn in a big company — how to run a community, how to talk to hardware vendors, how to make a hundred contributors from different companies agree on an architecture. That's not a bad fallback. And the upside is that this becomes the default serving engine for LLMs, and I helped build it from the inside. That asymmetry made the decision clearer than it probably looks from the outside.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the downside is bounded and describes a strong résumé and useful experience as a fallback, but does not identify a few years of forgone salary as the worst-case cost.

r002.rationale: The candidate says forming an entity would align incentives and support the project, but presents it as one model considered and does not state that starting a company was required for vLLM’s long-term development.

astra-6.text:
For me, the question was where I could have the most impact on vLLM. Starting a company could give me the freedom to focus on it, but running a company also means fundraising, hiring, and finding customers. That’s a different commitment from working on the technology.

Getting a job could offer stability and resources, especially if the role let me keep contributing to vLLM. So I wouldn’t frame it as entrepreneurship versus employment in the abstract. I’d ask which path would let me do useful work on the project sustainably, and whether there was a clear customer need that justified building a company.

r001.rationale: The response discusses startup commitments but does not say that failure would cost a few years of forgone salary.

r002.rationale: The response considers starting a company as one possible path, but does not state that vLLM’s long-term development required one.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, the main question was where I could have the most impact. A job would give me stability and an existing team to work with. Starting a company would mean more uncertainty, but it could also let me focus on supporting vLLM and helping people use it in production.

The difficult part is that enjoying open-source work doesn’t automatically mean you should start a company. You also need to understand what users need, what they would pay for, and whether you want the responsibility of building a business. So that’s how I’d frame the tradeoff: which path would let me do useful work sustainably?

r001.rationale: The response mentions uncertainty and a sustainable tradeoff, but does not state that a failed startup would cost a few years of forgone salary.

r002.rationale: It says starting a company could let him focus on supporting vLLM, but does not say he believed a company was necessary for vLLM’s long-term development.
